[[div class="blockquote" style="border-radius: 10px; margin: 10px"]] **Video Log Transcript** **Start time:** 20:36:53, 12 Mar 2018 ----- [BEGIN LOG] //The room is a modified break room, with several blackboards covering the walls, and a central conference table. The blackboards are full of writing, and there are papers spread across the table. There are two entities in the room, seated at the table a few chairs apart, each near a different stack of papers. The first is Sr. Researcher Angela Heinz, while the second is SCP-9216. Both are dressed in standard issue attire for researchers. Such attire is forbidden for SCP objects.// //At the beginning of the recording, Heinz is scribbling on a piece of paper, while SCP-9216 is reading a printout. SCP-9216 maintains the components of a general facial expression on the front of its head for the entire recording, and appears to display the same amount of focus as Researcher Heinz. After some time, SCP-9216 crumples up their paper and tosses it at Heinz, making a frustrated grunt. Its voice is roughly human.//   **SCP-9216:** Heinz, that's another dud. I'm telling you that this won't be on SCiPNET. It's conventional science. //Heinz looks up, scowling.// **HEINZ:** Already? We usually finish the internal review before you start moaning. **SCP-9216:** Internal review is for nonstandard science. This is plastics. I think they use plastics out in the real world. //Heinz snorts, and looks back at her scratchwork, muttering.// **HEINZ:** Fine, if you want to trawl civilian journals, then do it. I feel like I'm on to something here. //SCP-9216 looks at them for a moment, before getting up and exiting theory room 3. It returns roughly thirty seconds later, carrying a Foundation-issue laptop. Heinz does not look up as it sits back down, instead staring at her own page. SCP-9216 opens the laptop, and begins tapping the table impatiently as it starts up. After several minutes, it glances at Heinz.// **SCP-9216:** Your approach is working, you said? //HEINZ tosses her pencil down the table.// **HEINZ:** I said I thought I was on to something. **SCP-9216:** Something changed, then? **HEINZ:** Fine. Fine! I'll get my laptop, Vollard. [END LOG] [[/div]] [[size xx-large]]Item 1: AIC alert to Maria Jones[[/size]] [[include :scp-wiki:component:dynamic-emails start=-- |from=wilbur.aic@scp.int |to=jones@scp.int |cc=none |subject= ALERT: Compromised documentation, SCP-9216 ]] Director Jones, A routine audit of footage at Field Site W-8 has revealed evidence that documentation related to SCP-9216, an anomalous humanoid contained at the site, is of questionable integrity. I recommend RAISA personnel be sent to the site immediately. To re-establish the integrity of documents surrounding SCP-9216, I suggest agents be directed to answer the resolve the following issues I have found during my audit: # The subject is designated as Thaumiel, but the only listed reason for this in extant documentation is that the subject is cooperative, and has somewhat unusual physiology. This does not meet the standard 'Three-Step' Thaumiel criteria, and is at best a major error in classification by the subject's head researcher. # The supplementary files available to me are missing any record of the anomaly's acquisition. While some older anomalies simply have not digitized the physical paperwork and the Foundation allows physical copies to suffice, in this particular case I would like the copies digitized. # While there are abundant logs of SCP-9216's efforts in helping to contain other anomalous objects, tests of its own safety are minimal, which raises concerns when given the amount of exposure it has to other researchers, as well as to other anomalous objects. Were such tests ever done? # In footage from 12 March 2018, an employee, Senior Researcher Heinz, was observed referring to SCP-9216 as "Vollard." This is the surname of Senior Researcher Mary Vollard, who is also the head researcher on file for SCP-9216. In the same footage, SCP-9216 is seen to exit and re-enter theory room 3 using a Foundation key card at time 20:41:15. Site security logs confirm that SCP-9216 did so using Senior Researcher Mary Vollard's keycard. Why was SCP-9216 referred to with this surname, and why did a Foundation researcher permit an anomalous object to use a Level 3 keycard? [[include :scp-wiki:component:dynamic-emails end=-- |name=Wilbur.aic |title=RAISA automated search construct |signoff=Secure, Contain, Protect |signoff-icon=https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/local--files/component:dynamic-emails/transparent.png ]] [[size xx-large]]Item 2: Field Site W-8, new researcher Q&A[[/size]] Agent Will Ambrose arrived at Field Site W-8 on 14 March 2018, with a microphone and camera concealed on his person. His visit was unannounced, and was meant to gather information without alerting anyone to the active investigation. When he arrived, he found the site was holding an orientation for new employees, and opted to attend in order to learn more about the work culture on-site. When the various personnel were split into groups, Agent Ambrose chose to follow the session for new research staff. [[div class="blockquote" style="border-radius: 10px; margin: 10px"]] **Video Log Transcript** **Start time:** 10:03:22, 14 Mar 2018 ----- [BEGIN LOG] //The room is clearly meant for presentations, and at least fifty people are seated in rows before a projector. Agent Ambrose is standing by the rear door to the auditorium, and has a vantage of the whole room. He is facing the projector screen, which rolls up as people politely clap at the end of the "Site Clearances and You" presentation. Director Graham, a portly, balding man in his fifties, approaches the podium. He beams at the audience.// **GRAHAM:** Alright, everyone, we are coming up on the end of our orientation, and tomorrow you'll all be receiving your lab assignments. I know many of you are recent hires, and maybe you are nervous about jumping into lab work with the Foundation. Maybe you are curious about some of the differences I mentioned in how a field site is different from regular sites they taught you about in onboarding. Maybe you just have a question about site culture here. Well, whatever it is, we have this last hour reserved for a "no stupid questions" Q&A. I mean it. I'll explain the Foundation handbook if you want. We want you comfortable with the general stuff, because you would not believe the specifics you have to deal with at a Field Site. //A hand rises near the front of the room. Graham calls out to them.// **GRAHAM:** You, there. Speak up, now! **ATTENDEE:** Um, during the tours, our guide told us we can test dangerous stuff on an SCP we have here. Is that true? I thought cross-testing SCPs was banned. //Graham laughs, and turns to an agent by the front door. Graham motions at them, and the agent exits the room.// **GRAHAM:** Oh boy, that's the first question... five years running now! So, no, we do not test on an SCP, although, SCP-9216 is one of our most treasured containment assets at this site, and they are involved in testing here. Not tested on, though! //The agent returns to the room, and there are scattered gasps as SCP-9216 enters the room behind them. As before, it is dressed in standard Foundation researcher attire. It walks up to Graham's side, hands thrust in its pockets.// **GRAHAM:** Everyone, this is SCP-9216. She has assisted with more files than some of you will see in your entire careers here. Do you have anything you want to say to them? **SCP-9216:** Eh, hello everyone. I'm SCP-9216. You can call me that, it's fine, and yes, I tested, you can't catch... whatever I've got. I have been here a long time, doing research work, and I really don't want to see anyone get hurt. If you get something strange in your lab, or you just want some extra help, Director Graham put me on the site directory, somehow, and you can just message me there to ask if I can collaborate. Don't be shy. Is that good? **GRAHAM:** It's perfect. I'd recommend every one of you to consider her offer, there are a lot of researchers that owe their careers here to SCP-9216. Does anyone have any questions for her? ... no? Well, alright, you can go. Thank you for coming. **SCP-9216:** Of course. I'm sure I'll see some of you around. [END LOG] [[/div]] [[size xx-large]]Item 3: Excerpt from the personnel file of Sr. Researcher Mary Vollard, Director Graham's comments[[/size]] > **Annual review, 2010** > Another year of exemplary output from M. Vollard. She celebrated her 25th anniversary with the Foundation this past October, and it took some urging to get her to take a week off to enjoy the milestone. I am thankful she came back so quickly, though; one of the new hires had improperly stored what he failed to recognize as some Maxwellist tech in an unsecured server room, and M. Vollard caught it in her first hour back. Poor kid got his ear shouted off, but I can't say I can blame her. That's a good segue: > > We received three workplace complaints about M. Vollard since last year, down significantly from the seven we received when we lost H. Vollard in 2002. Two of the complaints came from younger, more inexperienced researchers, new enough to the site to get blindsided by her temper, and one came from A. Heinz. The latter was resolved with a third-party mediator, but I suspect it was just a stunt from A. Heinz to get under M. Vollard's skin, as per usual. Both parties declared the issue resolved, though, and the mediator signed off, so no disciplinary action was taken. > > M. Vollard also completed a training course on stewardship of sentient anomalous objects, as mandated by the Ethics Committee, following the loss of object B-2332 in a breach due to what the investigators termed "an overzealous containment response." I will not comment on the appropriateness of her response, but I stand behind M. Vollard as one of our most senior and trusted researchers, and stress to the committee the need for rapid action at a Field Site. I have faith she will continue to uphold Foundation principles going forward. [[size xx-large]]Item 4: Interview 1 with Director Graham[[/size]] Prior to this interview, Agent Ambrose had flagged a small assortment of files related to Field Site W-8 for review in order to conceal his interest in SCP-9216 specifically. Agent Ambrose claimed the files were flagged automatically by an outdated .AIC, and said he wished to confirm several details of the files with the director as a bureaucratic formality. The only relevant portion of the interview relates to SCP-9216 itself, which is excerpted below. [[div class="blockquote" style="border-radius: 10px; margin: 10px"]] **Video Log Transcript** **Start time:** 1:23:57, 14 Mar 2018 ----- [BEGIN LOG] **AMBROSE:** ... very good. Thank you for your patience so far, Director Graham. Now, next, I see... SCP-9216. Oh, yes, the Thaumiel. Between you and me, the file was probably just fine, but admin recently pushed out some new regulations, and now Wilbur is flagging anything that doesn't comply with a two-week old code. **GRAHAM:** Again? That must be on us, really sorry. We have been running lean for some time now, so it must have slipped by some of the researchers. I'll need to-- **AMBROSE:** It's fine, Director Graham. I'm here now, so why don't we step through the checklist together, and see what needs to be corrected? **GRAHAM:** By all means. **AMBROSE:** Wonderful. Now, let's see... First, Wilbur seems to have a problem with the Thaumiel designation itself, says it does not meet the Three-Step criterion. Are you familiar with that? **GRAHAM:** Can't say I am. Back when I was in the lab, I never did work on anything above Euclid. **AMBROSE:** That's quite alright. It just means that there is not enough information in the file about why SCP-9216 should be Thaumiel. It seems like the object has a talent for containment, but it isn't anomalous, and Thaumiels need to be anomalously good at containment, if that makes sense. **GRAHAM:**  Oh, oh, yes, I see. **AMBROSE:** So, what is the anomalous skill SCP-9216 has for containment? It is fine if there is none, it just means the object was filed back when we were more lax, and we can reevaluate it as needed, so-- **GRAHAM:** Oh, no, doesn't it say, in the file? It's very good, very good at Sarkic anomalies, you see. **AMBROSE:** Good at? **GRAHAM:** Oh, sorry, good at handling. I mean that, well, the anomaly is Sarkic itself -- perfectly safe of course, that should be in the logs -- **AMBROSE:** It is, yes. **GRAHAM:** -- and that makes it very resilient to other Sarkic anomalies. If you're already made out of putty, they can't really, ah, warp you more. **AMBROSE:** I see. Is there a reason this is not in the file? **GRAHAM:** It isn't? I'll have a word with the head researcher after this. **AMBROSE:** Senior Researcher Mary Vollard? **GRAHAM:** Yes, her. Excellent, wonderful employee, but not the best at administrative work. Some of the other files you asked me about are hers as well. She must have been getting worn out lately. I should have her workload lightened. **AMBROSE:** That would be a good idea. That aside, Wilbur also flagged the file as missing an acquisition record. He is being rather stubborn with it, so would it be possible for you to upload a copy of it? **GRAHAM:** Of course, it should be in storage somewhere. I'll ask Mary to handle that too. **AMBROSE:** Should I speak to her? That's two issues now that we can trace to her, so I could just walk her through the updated guidelines myself. **GRAHAM:** If you are still here when she has recovered, then sure. She's been out all week with a sprained ankle. **AMBROSE:** I see. Then please speak to her about those two issues, and also ask her to upload any remaining testing logs she has on SCP-9216 as addenda to the object file. Thaumiels now need a bit more information than is currently online, mainly to confirm the safety of the object, //especially// if the object will be interacting with other SCP objects. **GRAHAM:** Of course, I'll note that. **AMBROSE:** Thank you. Now, moving on... [END LOG] [[/div]] [[size xx-large]]Item 5: Conversation 1 between Director Graham and SCP-9216[[/size]] The following conversation was picked up by the security system of Field Site W-8, immediately following the conversation of Item 4. Director Graham was observed to enter SCP-9216's living quarters, and begin a conversation; due to SCP-9216's record of good behavior, no cameras were present within its living quarters. Accordingly, only parts of the resultant conversation were audible. [[div class="blockquote" style="border-radius: 10px; margin: 10px"]] **Video Log Transcript** **Start time:** 13:54:11, 14 Mar 2018 ----- [BEGIN LOG] //The dialogue is inaudible at first. Approximately 107 seconds after Director Graham entered, the subjects move closer to the doorway, and their conversation is picked up by a camera in the hallway.// **GRAHAM:** Well, he said it was just a formality, and we drew up a list of desired changes. **SCP-9216:** Even my file? **GRAHAM:** He had a few more things to say there, but otherwise, yes. He wanted a bit more information. Phrased it as their construct being finicky. **SCP-9216:** It's possible that's true, RAISA cares more about training specialists than getting the best software. They use Vim on the older machines there, I've heard... That can't be all. **GRAHAM:** He did ask to speak to Senior Researcher Mary Vollard. He wanted to help her make his requested edits. **SCP-9216:** Horseshit. I've never heard of an auditor going out of their way to speak to a researcher. Did you see his badge? **GRAHAM:** No first name listed. **SCP-9216:** Oh, oh no, that could be bad. The regular accountant types, they're level 2, I think. Full credentials on site visits for those. If he had a redacted card, he could be an actual investigator... **GRAHAM:** Really? Mary, paranoia isn't going to help here. **SCP-9216:** Two days after I get a lock on my file that I have never seen in my life, an agent from RAISA shows up. That's cause for paranoia! **GRAHAM:** And there's not a damn thing you can do about it. Just calm down, I'm on edge too and you're making me feel worse. Listen, I'll go talk to Angela. She's responsible for some of the flagged files, and she'll start making some edits to get everything on our end in order. I think we ought to fix everything we can, and give Mister Ambrose, whoever he is, no reason to stick around. **SCP-9216:** You're... you're right. Yes, you're right. Okay. I just need to make some edits... pace them out, get everything done timely, but not too timely. **GRAHAM:** That's all there is to it. **SCP-9216:** Yes... it's just strange to remember you can be an effective manager, when you need to be. **GRAHAM:** You're lucky I don't like writing people up, you know? //Graham exits SCP-9216's living unit, and calls back to it.// **GRAHAM:** We'll make it through this, Mary. See you tomorrow. [END LOG] [[/div]] [[size xx-large]]Item 6: Interview with Sr. Researcher Heinz[[/size]] [[div class="blockquote" style="border-radius: 10px; margin: 10px"]] **Audio Log Transcript** **Start time:** 12:08:13, 15 Mar 2018 ----- [BEGIN LOG] **AMBROSE:** I appreciate your fast response, Dr. Heinz. All of your entries seem to be fine now, and Wilbur should have lifted the edit lock by now. **HEINZ:** He did, a bit before I arrived. It makes me curious what this is about, Agent Ambrose. **AMBROSE:** Well, the number of flagged SCP entries for this site were a bit higher than normal. There can be any number of reasons for this. I wanted to check with a more experienced researcher to make sure that this was just random chance, and not, shall we say, symptomatic of some larger problem at the site. **HEINZ:** What? Agent, are you insinuating something? **AMBROSE:** Dr. Heinz, I am being open with you about concerns that RAISA has with your site -- concerns, I want to stress, that do not extend to you. You have a sterling record, and when I look at the site roster, Wilbur floated your name as one of the most loyal to the Foundation mission. If there is something unusual happening on site, I thought that you were one of the people here who would be be able to help us resolve it. **HEINZ:** Loyalty? Hah. I like doing research and having a secure place to do it. The Foundation provides that, so I like it here. I'm a bug happy with its nest, that's all. That said, what are you talking about with these... unusual happenings? All these flags were from those new regulations your people pushed out recently. People don't do paperwork fast, Agent Ambrose. That's not anomalous, so I don't know what you expect to hear. I think the lab rats down here collectively kicked their cans, but now we're caught up. That's all. **AMBROSE:** That's not true of all of Wilbur's flags. **HEINZ:** Ah? What's that mean? **AMBROSE:** Some files were in conflict with regulations as old as five years, and they all appear to be files belonging to Dr. Mary Vollard. **HEINZ:** Oh, of course she'd be making mistakes. **AMBROSE:** She is your colleague, correct? **HEINZ:** Oh, I babysit her from time to time, yes, when I have to catch her mistakes. I've been working with her since she transferred here, back in '92. You're saying we have this nice visit from RAISA because she forgot to format correctly? **AMBROSE:** In a way. It's rare for Wilbur to have strong reactions to existing files, but he even recommended a few of hers for Level 4 oversight. **HEINZ:** Hah! You know, we have a shared file, and she had the gall to tell me it was my fault it was flagged. My fault! She kept that up after I brought up the edit history, and showed her when she deleted Appendix D by accident. She's incorrigible. **AMBROSE:** Do you think the flags on her other files were due to similar accidents? **HEINZ:** Oh, likely. If you tell me which files Wilbur fingered, I could tell you more. **AMBROSE:** I cannot. Do you mind telling me the last time you spoke to Doctor Vollard in person? **HEINZ:** Oh. Heh. I get it now. **AMBROSE:** Doctor Heinz? **HEINZ:** Agent Ambrose, I have my problems with Mary, but I liked working with her husband. Have you ever read his file? **AMBROSE:** Is this relevant? **HEINZ:** Yes. He got posthumous honors, you know. It was a big deal. We have a plaque on site, dedicated to Henry Vollard for his heroism. **AMBROSE:** I was not aware. **HEINZ:** That's a shame. I would think a RAISA investigator would do some reading on the site they are assigned to beyond the case file. **AMBROSE:** I am just a -- **HEINZ:** Let me finish. This was back in the Omega-7 days, and every site had some related special project happening. I think if you had a few projects under your belt and submitted a proposal that had the word "cross-testing" in the abstract, you would get funding more often than not. Well, there was some prick on site, Roubel, who was gunning for the outgoing director's spot. He sent in this flimsy proposal that got greenlit. No idea what was in it, and Roubel waved us off whenever we asked for the details. He just kept getting shipments, level 4 classified, need-to-know. I was ready to start a fight with that grandstanding piece of shit when something got loose. It sent the whole site into lockdown. I just stayed put when the site security started blaring. I was on the other end of the site. Henry and Mary, though, they were right next to Roubel. I heard from others that Mary took the other researchers and went one way, while Henry went into Roubel's lab, and never came out. Neither did Roubel. **AMBROSE:** Riveting. What are you trying to tell me, Doctor Heinz? **HEINZ:** I'm just letting you know that Mary is a bitch, but her husband is better than a saint, he's a martyr. Whatever Roubel had in there was foul. They were forced to call in an MTF, and they started shooting as soon as they got in the lab. Whatever Henry did in there, O5 said he saved us all. He probably saved me. And despite all of that, Mary took a week of bereavement, and then came back to tend to her and Henry's projects. **AMBROSE:** Her husband sounds like an impressive man, but that does not exempt Mary Vollard from being investigated. There are genuine problems with her files, Doctor Heinz. **HEINZ:** Like with SCP-9216? **AMBROSE:** Would you care to explain why that file, in particular, comes to mind? **HEINZ:** No, I would not. Are you holding me for further questioning? **AMBROSE:** ... no, I am not. **HEINZ:** Then I believe our conversation is over. [END LOG] [[/div]] [[size xx-large]]Item 7: SCiPNET message from Angela Heinz[[/size]] The following message was sent approximately one hour after Agent Ambrose's interview with Angela Heinz. [[include :scp-wiki:component:dynamic-emails start=-- |from=afheinz49@scp.int |to=maryvollard@scp.int |cc=none |subject=re:re:re:re:re:fix supplement c dammit ]] Vollard, I just pushed new updates to the file. Read them and take them seriously. I just had a meeting with a RAISA agent who came by telling me you had terrible formatting in your other files, and that my formatting is much better. Maybe you should listen to me. He mentioned SCP-9216 is your worst. Just thought you should know where your failings are. Maybe you should pay special attention to it. [[include :scp-wiki:component:dynamic-emails end=-- |name=Angela Heinz |title=Senior Researcher, Field Site W-8 |signoff=Secure, Contain, Protect |signoff-icon=https://scp-wiki.wikidot.com/local--files/component:dynamic-emails/transparent.png ]] It was detected by Wilbur.aic shortly after being sent, who forwarded it to Agent Ambrose over suspicions of collusion; the message was not intercepted, since Wilbur.aic did not deem it to meet RAISA standards for actionable collusion. Agent Ambrose had Doctor Heinz placed on administrative leave for the remainder of the investigation, with her access to her accounts revoked in the interim. Agent Ambrose disputes that the above message did not constitute actionable collusion, and believes that Wilbur.aic is misreading RAISA bylaw 17.4.23. He has notified Director Maria Jones of the bylaw's imprecise wording, and Agent Ambrose recommends that it be rephrased, or that an internal memo be circulated clarifying its meaning. [[size xx-large]]Item 8: Interview 1 with SCP-9216[[/size]] After Sr. Researcher Heinz contacted Sr. Researcher Vollard, it was decided that Agent Ambrose should interview SCP-9216 as soon as was possible. As site administrators were suspected to be complicit in the database tampering, the interview was held before most site personnel arrive for work. [[div class="blockquote" style="border-radius: 10px; margin: 10px"]] **Video Log Transcript** **Start time:** 6:33:02, 15 Mar 2018 ----- [BEGIN LOG] //The video feed shows a type-II humanoid interview room, painted black as per code, with a single table and two chairs in the center. A door opens, out of view, and SCP-9216 enters, dressed in standard researcher attire, visibly upset. It takes a seat while scanning the room. Agent Ambrose follows it in, and takes the other chair. He pulls a legal pad out of his suit jacket along with a pen. SCP-9216 stares at him intensely.// **AMBROSE:** Now, let me say it again for the record: SCP-9216, my name is Agent Ambrose, and I am here from the Foundation's recordkeeping department. There have been some anomalies with the files at the site, and yours in particular has made us a bit confused. All I want to do is ask you a few questions about yourself, and get this all sorted out. **SCP-9216:** Okay. **AMBROSE:** Good. Let's go down your file. The first thing I see is the creation date, which is near the end of 2011. Is that when you first arrived here? **SCP-9216:** I think that's right. **AMBROSE:** Can you tell me about how you entered Foundation custody? **SCP-9216:** What do you mean by that? **AMBROSE:** I would like you to narrate the experience to me, SCP-9216. Modern regulations state that every file needs to have an acquisition record, and yours does not have one. **SCP-9216:** Do regulations allow you to just put down an SCP's word for their acquisition record? **AMBROSE:** They do not, but your word is a start. **SCP-9216:** There is not much to say. The Foundation is here and the GOC is all over this area. I needed some place to stay. That's all. **AMBROSE:** That's all? **SCP-9216:** What do you want me to say? How they gave me a room and started running tests? I complied. Of course I did. Every guard here has guns and tasers. **AMBROSE:** Well, then, may I ask what you were doing before you arrived here? **SCP-9216:** How long before? **AMBROSE:** Let's say the previous week. **SCP-9216:** I would prefer not to. **AMBROSE:** ... interesting. As a follow-up, I would like to ask another question about your past. Is this the physiology you were born with, or were you the victim of some sort of anomalous effect? **SCP-9216:** W-what? **AMBROSE:** Director Graham referred to you as a "sarkic anomaly" in conversation. That term raises some eyebrows, you see. **SCP-9216:** ... no, I was not born like this. **AMBROSE:** I see. Can you tell me about how your body came to be like this? **SCP-9216:** You're asking about something very unpleasant. Please, can we not discuss it? **AMBROSE:** We can come back to it. Instead, can you tell me what you did with your life before your body was like this? **SCP-9216:** Why are you doing this? **AMBROSE:** We need to complete your file, SCP-9216. It is missing so much right now. **SCP-9216:** Stop it. Do you think I'm an idiot? All these years and you can't even say what you mean to my face? I gave you bastards //decades.// Spit it out. //Ambrose puts his pen down and notepad down, and audibly sighs. Then, he stiffens, and stands.// **AMBROSE:** Pull your hands off the table. Now. **SCP-9216:** Huh? **AMBROSE:** Now! //SCP-9216 complies. Ambrose stares at the tabletop, and SCP-9216 follows his eyes.// **SCP-9216:** Oh, um, wait, this table is-- //Ambrose speaks into a microphone in his lapel; inaudible. The door opens, and site security enters. SCP-9216 is escorted from the room, as Ambrose remains; the anomalous entity does not resist.// //He waits for fifteen minutes before a field specialist in hazmat attire arrives in the room. The specialist takes several samples, and checks Ambrose for contamination. Until he is cleared to leave, Ambrose stares at the tabletop. Visible on the surface are two uneven handprints, freshly etched into the surface, on the far side of the table.// [END LOG] [[/div]] [[size xx-large]]Item 9: Summary of chemical findings[[/size]] After the preceding interview, SCP-9216's cell was examined. It contains several metal surfaces with which SCP-9216 makes frequent contact. Each displayed signs of chemical etching consistent with exposure to a weak acid, such as dilute hydrogen chloride. The site employs metal door handles, and in areas which SCP-9216 frequents, the same signs of etching were visible. Security footage from the interview was scoured, and it was verified that the table had no visible defects before the interview. The damage incurred was very shallow, only stripping the top layer of metal, but was still visible to the naked eye. Environmental testing determined this to be the result of a dilute solution of hydrochloric acid, with some organic compounds found in the human stomach mixed in. There are no mentions of chemical excretions in SCP-9216's file. [[size xx-large]]Item 10: Transcript of Mary Vollard on 7 August 2008, regarding Foundation policy[[/size]] Wilbur.aic discovered the following security footage of Field Site W-8's break room, which includes Sr. Researcher Vollard speaking about news from a sister site. Agent Ambrose deemed it relevant to the current investigation. [[div class="blockquote" style="border-radius: 10px; margin: 10px"]] **Video Log Transcript** **Start time:** 12:19:11, 7 Aug 2008 ----- [BEGIN LOG] //Sr. Researcher Vollard and Director Graham are alone at a table. They are both still eating, and speak between bites of food. Graham taps a printout on the table in front of them with his knuckles, drawing attention to it, while biting into his sandwich.// **GRAHAM:** Look at this. Remember Greeley, from before you transferred? **VOLLARD:** Mmm? Oh, him. Yeah, the xenobiologist. What is this? ... honored, employee of the month? Who'd he pay off? **GRAHAM:** No, no bribes. Just luck. I heard he got something classed Thaumiel. **VOLLARD:** Idiotic. He didn't even do anything. They bring the objects to you! **GRAHAM:** Well, it's still a Thaumiel. It's not easy to recognize the potential for one, that takes an eye. **VOLLARD:** An eye for recklessness? **GRAHAM:** What? **VOLLARD:** Did I stutter? **GRAHAM:** I get the feeling you aren't just talking about Greeley. **VOLLARD:** I'm not. Thaumiel was a mistake. It makes people look for magic bullets instead of doing honest science. It doesn't help when O5 lavishes the few good examples with praise. Oh, look at this, I don't know, indestructible box. Isn't it grand? If you ignore all the failures and the damage 76 did, then sure. I'm just afraid we're going to atrophy our research branches in favor of 'talent spotters' like Greeley. **GRAHAM:** So you'd never push for Thaumiel, huh? **VOLLARD:** You know, one of the junior researchers asked me that, back... oh, it must've been twenty years ago. **GRAHAM:** I'm surprised one of them wanted to talk to you. **VOLLARD:** He was new. Didn't know better yet. I had him amnesticized for using terms way above his clearance level, but before I did, I tore into him. I told him these things aren't his friends, never will be. Keep it behind the glass; don't let it //be// the glass. I thought that would be common sense... [END LOG] [[/div]] [[size xx-large]]Item 11: Interview 2 with Director Graham[[/size]] Agent Ambrose had an interview with himself inserted into Director Graham's schedule in order to discuss what had been discovered about SCP-9216. The site secretary was told to inform him of the meeting as soon as he arrived. [[div class="blockquote" style="border-radius: 10px; margin: 10px"]] **Video Log Transcript** **Start time:** 9:00:14, 16 Mar 2108 ----- [BEGIN LOG] //Director Graham's office. The director is sitting at his desk, staring ahead, when Agent Ambrose opens the door without knocking. He takes the seat in front of the director.// **AMBROSE:** Hello, director. **GRAHAM:** Agent Ambrose. **AMBROSE:** I wanted to talk to you about SCP-9216, as I am sure you're aware. Your cooperation will reflect well on you during the follow-up investigation. **GRAHAM:** I'm sure. **AMBROSE:** Indeed. Why isn't it recorded anywhere in SCP-9216's documentation that it can secrete a corrosive acid? **GRAHAM:** I'm not sure. **AMBROSE:** You are aware that this visit is a courtesy, correct? RAISA will learn the answer to that question, as well as any other question I might ask you. I am merely offering you the chance to offer it up and be acknowledged accordingly. I would urge anyone in a situation like yours to take advantage of such generosity. **GRAHAM:** I'm not being evasive. I didn't know she could do that. **AMBROSE:** Doubtful. **GRAHAM:** H-hey, listen here, I am being serious! Mary said she was sure there was no danger to anyone else, and I trust her! Why the hell would I go asking her for-- for a physical, or something? **AMBROSE:** Then, am I to believe that SCP-9216 is unaware of having such a capability? **GRAHAM:** Well... **AMBROSE:** Director Graham, are you about to say something reckless? **GRAHAM:** F-fine. There's... no way. She'd know. When she... when she first got like this, she spent months running all these tests. Every day, that was all she did. She wanted to make sure she was safe. I'm sure she would've learned something like that about herself. **AMBROSE:** Then, why are there only three entries on the testing logs for SCP-9216? **GRAHAM:** Because she isn't stupid. She... **AMBROSE:** Continue, Director Graham. You're doing a wonderful job. **GRAHAM:** She didn't want the file to have... rough edges. Nothing to make people want to double check it. Secreting acid, that sounds like it would raise eyebrows. Not that many, but, you know, maybe one person would take a second look. So she pared back the testing logs to the things that helped the... ah, the story she wanted to tell. **AMBROSE:** I see. As for yourself, director, why did you allow this? **GRAHAM:** Allow... Mary is one of the finest researchers we've ever had here. She's given her life to the Foundation. Are you asking... why I covered for her? **AMBROSE:** More or less. Regardless of how much I appreciate your cooperation, I am sure you realize this will, almost certainly, cost you your position. I also doubt that is a surprise to you. I am then asking why you bore such a risk. **GRAHAM:** Agent Ambrose, I've gotten so much from my career already. More than I deserve. If it happens, I won't see it as losing my job; I'll say I spent my job to give Mary eight years of security. The woman deserves it. **AMBROSE:** I see. That will be all, for now. Another agent will likely be in touch soon. **GRAHAM:** Whatever you say. [END LOG] [[/div]] Agent Ambrose had all privileges belonging to Senior Researcher Mary Vollard revoked, and had Director Graham placed on administrative leave for the remainder of the investigation, both effective immediately. He scheduled a meeting with SCP-9216 for the following day. [[size xx-large]]Item 12: Conversation 2 between Director Graham and SCP-9216[[/size]] Before he could be escorted out, Director Graham left his office, and met with SCP-9216 in its cell. The following conversation was recorded. [[div class="blockquote" style="border-radius: 10px; margin: 10px"]] **Video Log Transcript** **Start time:** 9:27:29, 16 Mar 2108 ----- [BEGIN LOG] //SCP-9216 is sitting at its desk, visibly frustrated, staring at a computer screen. It turns to see Director Graham approaching its cell.// **SCP-9216:** Richard, is SCiPNET down? This damn thing isn't working. **GRAHAM:** Oh, they already got to you. **SCP-9216:** What? What do... **GRAHAM:** I'm sorry, Mary. **SCP-9216:** Oh. I see. It's over? **GRAHAM:** I think so. He said I'll lose my job once this is all over, and he was splitting hairs over your documentation. You don't say stuff like that until the noose is good and tight. **SCP-9216:** I'm... I'm so sorry, Richard. **GRAHAM:** Don't worry about me right now. I just came to let you know. I also think I know the answer, but if there was a loss of power here, would you slip out? **SCP-9216:** Hah. This again? **GRAHAM:** Yes. Once they come for you, it's too late to leave. **SCP-9216:** It was too late to leave the first time my face melted off. I can't... buy groceries. I can't walk in the park. People would get called, and I'd hope it was the Foundation. Anyone else would be worse. **GRAHAM:** I thought so. **SCP-9216:** So don't do something stupid like throwing a breaker. They won't kill me. **GRAHAM:** It sounds like you wish they would. **SCP-9216:** What if I did? Do you think that will change things? You know how the-- how //we// work. Now it's all up to code. //Graham turns around, squinting.// **GRAHAM:** Did someone post guards here? **SCP-9216:** Of course they did, this is an active investigation. Leave, you idiot! **GRAHAM:** It's always been a pleasure, Mary. Goodbye. //Graham exits, and footsteps pass outside. SCP-9216 stands, glancing at a passing guard, and then returns to its bed. It closes all its eyes.// [END LOG] [[/div]] By noon, Acting Director Stephen Goff had taken control of the site. [[size xx-large]]Item 13: Interview 2 with SCP-9216[[/size]] [[div class="blockquote" style="border-radius: 10px; margin: 10px"]] **Video Log Transcript** **Start time:** 8:05:22, 17 Mar 2108 ----- [BEGIN LOG] //SCP-9216 is led into the same interview room as used in Item 8 of this investigation, with the same damaged table in place. It stares at the handprints on the surface, before settling into its chair. Soon after, Agent Ambrose enters, and seats himself opposite.// **SCP-9216:** Hello. **AMBROSE:** Hello, SCP-9216. I am hopeful this interview is the last piece of evidence I will need for my report, if you can just follow along with a few formal steps. Your compliance, of course, will be noted in the final report. **SCP-9216:** Okay. **AMBROSE:** Wonderful. Now, first, I suspect you have a Foundation keycard in your possession. May I have it? **SCP-9216:** Oh. You're very direct. **AMBROSE:** Is there any point to discretion anymore? **SCP-9216:** I suppose not. //SCP-9216 reaches into its pocket, pulling out a card which it places on the table. Ambrose holds it up, in view the camera.// **AMBROSE:** Let the record show that this is the keycard belonging to Senior Researcher Mary Vollard. Now, SCP-9216, I am already certain of the answer, but could you state on the record why you have this keycard? **SCP-9216:** Because it's mine. Is that what you want to hear? **AMBROSE:** That seems to imply that you were previously in Foundation employ as Senior Researcher Mary Vollard. Are you claiming that to be the case? **SCP-9216:** Yes, I am. **AMBROSE:** That is very troubling, SCP-9216. Do you have proof of this fact? If not, you should be aware that impersonating a Foundation official is tantamount to an escape attempt, and will be treated accordingly. **SCP-9216:** It's... there should be footage. Of the... the event. Check, oh, the security cameras from... August, mid August of 2011. Testing room 7. I think. //Ambrose stands and walks to the door of the interrogation room. He opens it, leaning out to talk to a guard stationed outside, and then returns to his seat opposite SCP-9216.// **AMBROSE:** We're going to have the footage combed. It should take a few hours at most to find this incident, assuming you are telling the truth. However, I would like you to tell me what we are going to find. **SCP-9216:** W-what? Why? **AMBROSE:** To verify it is you we will see in the footage, and not some other impostor, with improbable anatomy. I do want to say that compliance will reflect well on you. **SCP-9216:** Oh, fine. Just... give me a moment. **SCP-9216:** Okay. Alright. There was a new researcher, Evans. Pale, not even thirty, wispy blonde hair. He was anxious... I think he was only starting to realize what we do here. The new ones tended to come to me and Heinz. The other old boys were too intimidating, I guess. Evans was nicer than the others, always said please, very meek... **SCP-9216:** Anyways, he came to me one day, panicking. He was assigned to intake, which was a mistake: junior researchers can't onboard new objects without a supervisor. That meant Graham f--... that meant Graham made a mistake, since he was still getting used to the scheduling software. I was mad, and just about stormed up to Graham's office, but Evans said that wasn't the issue. The kid had started unboxing anomalous objects, thinking he was supposed to know enough to handle it, and dropped something. He was about to puke, and could barely choke out that he chipped a statue. **SCP-9216:** Technically, you know, he shouldn't have left the room. There are intercoms in there, and if anything happens, you radio out, and someone is supposed to come help you. Evans... well, he couldn't have known that. He was a junior researcher! He wasn't trained to do intake, so how the hell would he know what we do? I sent him off to decontamination, maybe raising my voice a bit too much, but I was focused on getting to the testing room so I could do cleanup. **SCP-9216:** I rushed in there, and like Evans said, there was a half-unloaded box on the table, and a little marble statue on the ground, with a few shards chipped off of it. It looked Greek. It was this figure on a square base, and it looked so ugly. A bunch of limbs and flesh, it just screamed sarkic, and it was done in a classical, detailed style. Like Michaelangelo. There was something written on the base, and I looked it up a long time later: it was a quote from Heraclitus. "Everything flows." **AMBROSE:** Did you spend a long time studying the object? **SCP-9216:** Oh, no. It was a few seconds, but this was a memorable day for me. **AMBROSE:** Alright, please continue. **SCP-9216:** Well, I only had a few seconds because my arm started tingling, and then it started to bend where I thought there should be bone. My forearm must have already gone, by that point, and I wasn't used to holding myself together. I threw the statue back on the table, and I already knew this was very bad. Chipping the statue must have exposed something, I remember thinking. I also remember something splattering against the ground to the side of me, at the same time my arm felt a lot lighter. **SCP-9216:** I didn't really want to look. You might think I was panicking, but I wasn't, though what was going through my head wasn't much better. It was rage. I thought, wow, this is it? Some anomaly is going to take the last things I had left from me? I am going to die in here, a puddle of... something, and that's it? **AMBROSE:** You didn't realize the anomaly wouldn't kill you? **SCP-9216:** No, not at all. Whenever I'd seen something that extreme happen to a colleague, I lost that colleague. I thought the same thing would happen to me. I thought those were my last moments. I saw Evans had left out his flasks, and one of them was decently high molar hydrochloric acid, so with the little time I thought I had... heh, it sounds so stupid. I grabbed that flask with my good arm, and I knocked it over, on the statue. At least it would be a draw that way: we'd both be slurry. Then my legs turned to mush, and before my ears went, I heard the sizzle of the marble being eaten away. **AMBROSE:** Is that all? **SCP-9216:** Oh, more or less. I was ooze when they found me. They put me in a container, and then assigned me to Heinz. They weren't sure I was still in there until I figured out how to respond to sensory tests a few days later. **AMBROSE:** That sounds to be beyond what the footage will include, so you can stop there. What about this junior researcher, Evans? Was he affected? **SCP-9216:** No. They checked the footage, and he was running for the door before the statue hit the ground. Whatever was in it didn't have time to disseminate while he was still there. **AMBROSE:** Sounds reasonable. Well, that's the last box I needed to check to conclude the investigation. Thank you very much for you cooperation. //Ambrose begins to stand.// **SCP-9216:** What is going to happen to me? **AMBROSE:** Hm? Isn't that obvious? You'll be reclassified properly, and recontained somewhere else. Likely with restricted privileges. **SCP-9216:** Is there any chance I can remain here, and keep working? **AMBROSE:** Someone with as much experience as yourself should know better than to ask that. Besides, it is not Foundation policy to explain our containment protocols to the objects we contain. **SCP-9216:** After all I've been through, can't you humor me? //Ambrose sits back down.// **AMBROSE:** After all you've been through? Do you mean transgressing for eight years against Foundation codes that you yourself once followed? Or, do you mean creating a tangled mess that I have spent the past week teasing apart? If you wanted preferential treatment, you should not have falsified your file. **SCP-9216:** You really think that would have made any difference? **AMBROSE:** Pardon? **SCP-9216:** I really doubt the Foundation would have treated me any different if I had surrendered at the start. I think they would've boxed me up and shipped me off just the same. There's an old Ethics Committee guideline about that: attacking staff should be punished, but the Committee recommended forgiveness, and lighter sentences, when there's a peaceful containment breach. **AMBROSE:** ... I have, perhaps, read that guideline. **SCP-9216:** So, if you're saying it's not worth even thinking about me staying here now... there was never a hope. In fact, my chances should be better, since I've proven that I can still do the work like this, but you still think it's not going to happen. **AMBROSE:** That was only my opinion. My involvement with your future is only to file this report. **SCP-9216:** You could make a recommendation, couldn't you? **AMBROSE:** Why should I? If I may be direct, you selfishly put this entire facility at risk because you wanted to pretend your life was the same as before. You compromised a slew of Foundation documents, and through this investigation, are wasting resources on cleaning up your mess. You seem like a drain on the Foundation, not an asset. **SCP-9216:** You fucking worm. **AMBROSE:** Again, you are not endearing yourself to the -- **SCP-9216:** You have the gall to say //I'm// a drain on the Foundation? I gave more to the Foundation than you ever will! No, I let the Foundation //take// more from me than you ever will, because I //believed// in it! My youth, my-- my family, my chance at kids, no hobbies, no more love, no more sun on my skin, even the... the face in the mirror. Gone. All because I wanted to spare others. Because I wanted to keep them from what I had to face. I was locking up monsters, and because the Foundation made a //mistake//, and let some poor kid in a room with something scary, now I get caged up too? You don't think they should have shame? You wretched sack of shit. I gave more than my life to this place, and even when that life was gone, I kept giving, and giving, and giving! **AMBROSE:** You compromised the entire site. **SCP-9216:** What the hell does that even mean? I bet the Foundation won't change a single word of what I put in all those files I made, because it's damn good work and they know it! They'll just try and paper over me, so they can pretend they didn't just throw me away like a fucking candy wrapper when I needed them! **AMBROSE:** SCP-9216, you are out of line! Be quiet! //SCP-9216 glares at Agent Ambrose, but goes silent. He stares back at her.// **AMBROSE:** The Foundation is not a storefront. It does not trade labor for recognition, or respect. It trades it for money, as every employer does. You tell me that you "gave" many things to the Foundation? That's called a job. You were compensated for everything you gave. In fact, you will be compensated one more time, as your Foundation life insurance policy will pay out to your next of kin as soon as the investigation concludes. **SCP-9216:** You, you--! //SCP-9216 grimaces, and clenches its misshapen hands. It trembles, and pulls them close to its chest.// **SCP-9216:** Oh, this is pointless, isn't it? **AMBROSE:** Pardon? **SCP-9216:** Fighting. I really should know better. I know what I did when objects resisted like I just did: more bars, less amenities. Never more freedom. **AMBROSE:** Treating anomalous objects like that sounds like a violation of Foundation guidelines. Thankfully for you, the Foundation will not punish you over transgressions from when you were in Foundation employ. Is that reassuring? **SCP-9216:** You know, Agent Ambrose, you really are a model employee. Ah... //SCP-9216 looks down, placing its hands on the table. It fiddles with its digits; it has eleven, at the time of the recording.// **SCP-9216:** ... this reminds me of when Henry died. I inherited all his projects, you know. It was a lot of paperwork, getting the names changed on everything. At the end, I had to meet with a RAISA agent to certify everything, and get the new cards. I remember he acted a lot like you. When I told him I was sorry for taking so long to finish, since I was handling the funeral, he just said, "it's fine." Not a word more about me, not sorry for my loss, nothing. I think I understand him now. He was just there to complete his job, and it didn't need him to understand or feel a thing about me. To him, there may as well have been nothing there in the chair opposite him. //Agent Ambrose shifts in his chair.// **AMBROSE:** He was likely from accounting, not investigations. A different department. **SCP-9216:** He's probably been promoted by now. He seemed like a good worker, focused on the job. The kind the Foundation likes. **AMBROSE:** I think we're done here. //Ambrose stands, pausing when he sees SCP-9216 is crying. It is staring at him.// **SCP-9216:** Agent Ambrose, I bet you'll be up for promotion soon. This investigation, you've managed it so well. I really had no chance. It'll reflect well on you. **AMBROSE:** Perhaps. There's no way of knowing. **SCP-9216:** Other people will ask you about this case, at least. **AMBROSE:** Likely. Why do you mention it? **SCP-9216:** Well, I just wanted to ask a stupid favor. If someone asks what the case was about, please don't tell them it was about SCP-9216. Just... say it was about Mary Vollard. **AMBROSE:** I don't think I can-- **SCP-9216:** Please. **AMBROSE:** ... once it is revised, I will leave a note on your file about how you prefer to be addressed. Goodbye, SCP-9216. //Agent Ambrose exits the room. SCP-9216 remains seated, staring at the door, until site security arrive to take it away.// [END LOG] [[/div]] **SUBMITTED TO RAISA DIRECTOR MARIA JONES ON 22 MARCH 2018** **PENDING RECLASSIFICATION** [[/collapsible]] [[footnoteblock]] [[div class="footer-wikiwalk-nav"]] [[=]] << [[[SCP-9215]]] | SCP-9216 | [[[SCP-9217]]] >> [[/=]] [[/div]]

    ⚠️ Content warning: This article features alcohol consumption, severe psychological distress, and panic attacks.

Item#: 9219
Level1
Containment Class:
neutralized
Secondary Class:
none
Disruption Class:
dark
Risk Class:
danger
link to memo

Special Containment Procedures: Following its restoration by a Foundation front company, the location of SCP-9219's occurrence was monitored for 30 days. The at-first fluctuating Hume levels have since stabilized. As SCP-9219 is believed to have been a one-time event, no further measures are currently planned. All records of the anomaly's presence have been confiscated.

Description: SCP-9219 refers to the events that occurred on [REDACTED] 2025 in an attic in [REDACTED], Hamburg, Germany (see Addendum 1).

SCP-9219-1 describes the suspected perpetrator of these events, one Martin Feldt. It is believed that Feldt was a reality bender, but whether he was aware of this remains unclear. Investigations into his background have yielded no information. Feldt was 27 years old at the time of his demise and a carpenter by trade. He had never previously come to the attention of the Foundation or public authorities.

Update: Persistent odors of smoke within the attic in question are to be explained as harmless residues from the fire.

Addendum 9219-A: Log of SCP-9219's Occurrence

DATE: [REDACTED]

LOCATION: Attic in [REDACTED], Hamburg, Germany

FOREWORD: The following log has been derived from the analysis of damaged security camera footage. Due to the poor original quality and the absence of audio recordings, only fragmentary dialogues could be extracted via lip-reading.

The attic belonged to Martin Feldt's apartment, one floor below. He apparently used it for leisure activities with his group of friends.

[Begin Log]

[The attic is on display. Its furnishings resemble a small living room, including two windows, couches, garlands, and plastic plants. Beverage crates and gaming consoles can be seen next to a television.]

17:41: A person enters. Based on the reddish hair, lanky stature, and pale complexion, it is confirmed to be Martin Feldt. He places his phone on the couch table and walks to one of the two sloped roof windows, gazing outside. He is periodically seen kneading his hands absentmindedly.

17:45: With a thoughtless motion, Feldt's right sleeve touches the chest of drawers between the two windows. A deck of cards lying there falls down. The cards scatter across the floor. Feldt looks down at them abruptly. He doesn't move.

17:46: The cell phone presumably emits a signal tone as Feldt suddenly turns to look at it. He moves toward the table and retrieves it to read a message.

17:47: He sighs, puts the cell phone down again, and collects the cards. As he approaches them, he opens and closes his hands several times. He places the collected cards on the couch table.

[Twenty-four minutes pass as Feldt cleans the room, presumably in anticipation of guests. He then proceeds to sit on the couch with his phone. Feldt opens and scrolls through several social media pages.]

18:12: It appears that the doorbell rings, as Feldt looks toward the door and stands. The camera captures him closing open apps, including a YouTube video about mental health.

18:14: Three newcomers enter the room: Annalena Kirchhofer (26, graphic designer), Fabian Seitz (27, railway employee, Kirchhofer's partner), and Maximilian Beck (26, florist). Greetings and hugs are exchanged.

18:14: The camera feed experiences brief interference but stabilizes after 8 seconds.

18:17: The group gathers on the two couches. They discuss the weather, a recent soccer game, and then personal news. Feldt occasionally gives nonverbal signs of agreement and, when addressed by Kirchhofer, shrugs his shoulders once before fetching drinks for those present. Beck begins showing the group a series of memes on his phone, to everyone's amusement.

18:39: Feldt suddenly looks across the room for seven seconds, where the television, a desk, and a cabinet are located. He stands up and moves in that direction, but then slows and turns left to open a window.

18:40: Seitz prompts Feldt to turn on the television and a console. Feldt does so without hesitation. He then points to the controllers next to the couches. As everyone present focuses their attention there for four seconds, Feldt's shadow stretches unnaturally across the parquet floor and bends toward the cabinet before resettling.

[The group begins playing. Feldt sits on the right-hand couch, while the other three occupy the other one. All present commence drinking beer from the storage boxes in the process. Feldt is partially out of view, but can be seen repeatedly checking his phone instead of partaking.]

18:58: Kirchhofer prompts Feldt to take a controller. He declines. She inquires as to his mood and well-being. A draught pushes the half-open window further open. The closet door rattles.

18:58: Feldt gestures casually towards Kirchhof. He explains that he is feeling a little under the weather and moves to the window, closing it. Upon turning, he suggests ordering pizza. The group agrees after some mostly ironic debate on the details of the order.

19:05: While the others continue to follow the games, Feldt orders via his phone. As he finishes, he looks for the spare controller on the couch table.

19:05: Kirchof invites him to join again. They exchange a smile.

19:05: Without any visible influence, the cards previously placed on the table fall off the edge. Feldt freezes, Beck notices the cards but picks them up without commenting.

19:07: Feldt still has not moved. He remains tense.

19:08: What appear to be ice crystals are seen forming on Feldt's clothing and skin. The others do not appear to notice.

19:09: The air directly around Feldt begins to shimmer. The ice rapidly evaporates. The group does not react, but cheers on the ongoing game.

19:10: The ceiling light flickers twice, then begins to pulse with increasing frequency. Feldt remains motionless.

19:11: The cabinet door shakes.

19:12: Feldt's left hand tightens on his knee.

19:12: A spatial anomaly occurrs. The room is warping along the X-axis from north to south. The structures of the walls and floor move in conflicting directions. Despite the circumstances, the others present seem oblivious. Kirchhof makes a joke about the air quality and suggests opening the window again. The room contracts.

19:14: The rotation through the center of the room approaches 40 degrees. Feldt does not move. Drawers, bottle caps, the door, and the cabinet doors are tightly sealed by an invisible force.

19:14: The whole cabinet is seen vibrating.

19:15: Feldt opens his mouth as he stares ahead. He does not speak. The room settles back to its normal form. The light is pulsing in deep, quick flashes.

19:16: The floor dents inward. An expanding hole appears. It expands until Feldt is sitting on its edge. Neither his friends nor he react to this.

19:17: The group cheers at the game again.

19:17: Feldt's lips tremble, but he does not appear to speak.

19:18: The cupboard suddenly opens. Visible inside are cleaning products and a vacuum cleaner. A person who appears to be identical to Feldt steps out. He is furthermore wearing a rainbow-colored band on his right wrist.

19:18: The figure steps to the opposite edge of the hole.

19:18: Feldt and his double stare at each other. Neither speaks.

19:18: Doubes of Kirchhof, Seitz, and Beck stand up, while the presumed originals remain seated. They stand still for a moment, then point to the Feldt double.

19:18: The Feldt-double plunges into the hole in one fluid motion and disappears. The hole closes.

19:19: The room deforms again, toward Feldt. Sharp edges and points begin to move toward him.

19:19: The remaining three doubles turn toward Feldt. Their expressions warp until their faces are unrecognizable. They abruptly vanish.

19:21: Kirchof, still unaware, turns to Feldt.

19:21: Kirchhof touches Feldt's shoulder. All movement stops.

19:21: Kirchhof asks Feldt what is up with him.

19:21: Feldt looks at her. Kirchhof's expression changes to concern.

19:22: The lightbulb bursts. Beck is hit by the splinters and recoils.

19:22: Seitz screams upon realising the room's unnatural state. Pipes and cables burst through the wall and begin wrapping around Feldt in rapid succession.

19:22: The room commences falling in on Feldt, who remains sitting motionless.

19:23: Kirchhof is seen reaching for Feldt.

19:23: All objects and structures then suddenly invert their trajectory within moments, but do not fully return to their normal state.

19:23: The cabinet doors fly open again. A mass of fire erupts into the room.

19:23: Feldt jumps up and stretches his arms toward the blaze. It visibly slows down.

19:23: Feldt seems to realize what he is doing. He looks at the other three, who are staring at him.

19:23: Beck, open-mouthed, raises a hand and points at Feldt.

19:23: Feldt freezes.

19:24: All present are engulfed in the flames. The fire alarm triggers.

[End Log]

CONCLUSION: The Hamburg fire department arrived in a timely manner and brought the fire under control, but the attic burned down completely. All present lost their lives; however, SCP-9219-1's remains are still unaccounted for.

The Foundation only became aware of the incident through comments exchanged between the police and fire department via telephone regarding unusually deformed objects and furnishings, and subsequently intervened. As far as is known, however, the incident did not attract further attention and was dismissed as a fire caused by a faulty gas pipe.

According to investigations by Foundation personnel, it is in fact probable that the fire was caused by electrical and gas lines accidentally damaged by SCP-9219, and not intentionally by SCP-9219-1 directly. Further investigations revealed that the building's infrastructure was outdated and dilapidated.

Take a deep breath, and I'll lift the mask… Ready?

  • 

    close

    Info

    X

    This article was written by Deadcanons as part of Anthology 2025.

    ⚠️ Content warning: Body horror, mutilation, medical trauma, gender-related mutilation, sexual assault, physical assault, blood loss/mass hemorrhage, pregnancy trauma, suicide, infanticide

⚠️ content warning

Item #: SCP-9220

Object Class: Euclid

Special Containment Procedures: Pregnancy records of all maternity wards worldwide are to be monitored for keywords such as "immaculate", "spontaneous", and "miraculous." If keywords are discovered, at least one Foundation agent must be stationed at the associated maternity ward until it can be confirmed that no cases of SCP-9220 are present at the facility.

Per Ethics Committee memorandum, any identified mothers must be given the explicit option to abort the fetus. If the mother chooses to carry the SCP-9220-A instance to term, the Foundation agent is to assume the role of the mother's primary obstetrician and assign regular check-ups. Upon delivery, the SCP-9220-A instance is to be immediately removed from the facility and brought to Site-22.

While the mother is convalescing in recovery, Class C amnestics are to be administered, targeting all memories associated with the pregnancy. Class C must also be administered to the immediate family within 1-2 weeks.1

All instances of SCP-9220-A are to be kept at Site-22, in a specially prepared cold storage chamber. Each instance is to be strapped to a medical table and fitted with a standard hospital gown. Once a week, a researcher must remove the gown and thoroughly inspect the instance for new growths and bodily changes.

Any instance which has been in Foundation containment for a period greater than 21 years is to be removed from cold storage and moved to a standard humanoid containment chamber. Once activity is confirmed, the attending researchers are to follow the steps outlined in Addendum 9220.4.

Description: SCP-9220 is a condition effecting approximately 0.00001%2 of humans bearing maternal organs. SCP-9220 manifests as spontaneous pregnancy, in many cases without any prior evidence of conception.

All babies produced from SCP-9220 are born dead. These corpses, hereafter referred to as instances of SCP-9220-A, display advanced stages of dehydration and desiccation. SCP-9220-A appear to have been dead from well before the time of birth, and show no signs of heartbeat, brain waves, or other metabolic functions. In spite of this, instances will continue to grow and age at a rate equivalent to a living human.

Upon reaching a point hereby referred to as the Terminal Age (approx. 21 years), the instance will open their eyes and [DATA EXPUNGED]. Out of the ██ thousand documented cases that have reached this stage, approximately 6% are currently used by the Foundation for testing, therapy, and other classified responsibilities, as assigned by the Department of Massage Therapy. The other 94% [DATA EXPUNGED].

Addendum 9220.2: SCP-9220-A-607, "HASID"

Instance: SCP-9220-A-607, "HASID"
Assigned researcher(s): Annabelle Kraken, Harelyn Steel, Xir Lin Sun

[DOB CLASSIFIED]: In spite of signature SCP-9220 characteristics, -A-607 was delivered at a healthy weight of 2.920 kg (6 pounds 7 ounces). Further investigation has revealed the presence of a heavy growth in -A-607's abdomen.

1 y.o.: Instance maintains steady growth, while no changes have been observed in the object in its abdomen. Body remains unusually heavy. Researcher Kraken requests approval to draw an intravenous sample from the growth. Request approved.

Kraken successfully draws 3 mL of living red blood cells from the abdomen. Researcher Steel requests approval to perform an ultrasound. Request approved.

1 y.o.: Ultrasound confirms that the growth in the abdomen is an undeveloped fetus. Size is extremely small and is analogous to less than a week of development in a healthy pregnancy. A corpus luteum3 is present in the ultrasound. The umbilical cord is highly developed and represents the majority of the instance's additional weight.

Control samples of blood were drawn from the abdomen and thigh. As is to be expected from instances of SCP-9220-A, there is no blood in the body. However, researchers were again able to draw a small sample of blood from the umbilical cord.

5 y.o.: The fetus shows no development.

10 y.o.: The fetus shows no development.

15 y.o. Fetus may have developed, but it is impossible to tell due to the relatively small size at this stage in development (fetus is smaller than a grain of rice). Researcher Sun requests weekly ultrasound schedule. Request approved.

15 y.o.: A heartbeat is detected in the fetus. Effective immediately, all further activity with this project requires the direct approval of the O5 Council.

　

While many of the details of SCP-9220-A-607's pregnancy are classified under NEED-TO-KNOW designation, the following timeline has been approved for Level 4 Clearance. For the sake of clarification, -A-607 is referred to by the codename of "HASID," and the fetus is referred to by the codename of "CHESED."

First Trimester (1-12 weeks)

CHESED's heartbeat weakens rapidly in the days after first detection. Primary care team (Rsrs. Sun, Kraken, and Steel) request permission to intravenously provide blood to the umbilical cord via the insertion of an artificial vein in HASID's lower back. Request approved. HASID is moved to a modified observation table which allows for the upper body to rest at an incline. Holes in the back of the table, and between the legs, allow for easy access to the back and abdomen. Shortly following surgery, CHESED's heartbeat can be detected normally again.

Less than a week later, the artificial vein collapses. Steel theorizes this is due to the lack of musculature supporting it. A new artificial vein is inserted directly through the belly button. A specially-designed "muscle" made of silicone and wiring is wrapped around HASID's abdomen. The "muscle" pulses regularly, simulating the natural contractions of organic tissue.

At 11 weeks, Sun reports active brain waves coming from CHESED. Ultrasounds show clearly-developed organs and limbs. Prenatal test confirms that CHESED is female.

Second Trimester (13-27 weeks)

Fetus shows late signs of placental insufficiency. The corpus luteum, which should have detached by week 12, is still attached to the uterine lining and is no longer producing progesterone. The placental structure has not grown to replace the corpus luteum. Due to these insufficiencies, HASID has not produced an amniotic sac or amniotic fluid suitable for supporting CHESED's development.

Kraken proposes the installation of a modified pump around HASID's vaginal opening. The pump will serve to both seal the womb for CHESED's protection, as well as provide a way of introducing artificial amniotic fluid into CHESED's environment. Approved.

During installation, an artificial semipermeable membrane is pushed through the pump and expanded within HASID's uterus. Ultrasound confirms that CHESED is successfully engulfed by the membrane. The membrane is then pumped full of a modified Ringer's lactate solution consisting of sodium chloride, sodium lactate, potassium chloride, calcium chloride, water, and [DATA EXPUNGED].

During week 15 ultrasound, Steel reports that CHESED performed a roll by kicking off the side of the artificial sac.

During week 17 ultrasound, Kraken reports the muffled sound of CHESED giggling.

Prior to week 19 ultrasound, Sun requests approval to bring simple audio recordings (e.g. forest sounds, a field recording of a crowded park, classical music, etc.) into the observation chamber for the sake of CHESED's development. Request approved.

Third Trimester (28-40 weeks)

During week 28 ultrasound, CHESED is observed sleeping soundly. This behavior is to be expected of a baby in the third trimester.

At the start of week 33, Sun reports that HASID's decay has progressed suddenly. Deep purple bruising is visible on both sides of HASID's body, in the approximate positions of the liver and kidneys. Increased decay has never before been observed in an instance of SCP-9220-A.

After inspection, Steel theorizes that HASID's apparently healthy umbilical cord is attempting to circulate waste products from CHESED out of HASID's bloodstream. HASID's lack of functioning circulatory system would cause the blood to stagnate, resulting in a form of late-stage livor mortis. Concerns are expressed by the team that if left untreated, the body may fall apart due to blood pooling.

Proposals are made to remove the artificial womb from the body, with the umbilical cord still attached for the remainder of the pregnancy. Kraken protests due to the continued damage the umbilical cord will cause to HASID. Sun becomes incensed at the implication that HASID's corpse is of equal value to CHESED's ongoing survival. Kraken begins to describe a theoretical model for an artificial umbilical cord, but is cut off by Steel, who cites the 0% success rate of artificial human pregnancies. Kraken cites the higher success rate of artificial animal pregnancies, and states that the Foundation is inherently more capable than any Veiled group of scientists.

Sun again asserts that the discussion is irrelevant due to the fact that only one of the subjects in question is actually alive. Kraken becomes agitated and references SCP-9220-A-522, stating that "You [Sun] didn't have to watch your baby go through that." Sun begins crying. At this point, HASID's right arm falls off the observation table and snaps off of the body above the elbow. Kraken shouts an expletive and leaves the room.

Following a two-day recess, the O5 Council orders the team to proceed by removing the artificial womb from HASID while leaving the umbilical cord in-tact. The team is given explicit permission to remove the artificial womb without regard to the state of HASID, and is permitted to completely sever the pelvic floor if necessary. Under protest from Kraken, the right arm is disposed of.

During surgery, Steel successfully performs a cesarean cut to HASID's abdomen, but is unable to remove the artificial sac due to the rigid state of the dried tissue. Steel expresses concern that the only way to remove the sac is by completely cutting open HASID's torso. Sun urges him to proceed. Kraken remains silent. Steel appears uncomfortable and excuses himself, stating he needs to "think about this."

Sun picks up the surgery tools and declares her intention to continue with the operation. Kraken remains silent. Sun opens the cesarean cut down to HASID's vaginal opening, eviscerating the front of the body. She is still unable to remove the artificial sac. Sun states aloud that she is going cut horizontally in order to further open up the torso.

The resulting conversation between Sun and Kraken has been struck from the record.

Sun proceeds by making two horizontal cuts on the upper and lower abdomen, starting at the cesarean cut. Sun then uses her hands to forcibly widen the opening. She is able to remove the artificial sac without further difficulty. CHESED can be seen within the membrane and is sleeping. She moves restlessly in her sleep.

Delivery

CHESED was delivered by the containment team prematurely on week 34. The decision was made to remove CHESED early due to the rapid deterioration of HASID, which presented difficulties in carrying the baby to full term. Additionally, the team expressed concerns that decaying matter from HASID's corpse could become incorporated with the blood circulating through the umbilical cord, causing harm to CHESED.

The research team anticipated complications during delivery, namely in the sudden decrease of oxygen CHESED would receive to the brain following the severing of the umbilical cord. To combat birth asphyxia, a therapeutic hypothermia chamber was prepared and fitted as a nursery for CHESED's early development. The nursery was prepared by members Site-22's Department of Massage Therapy. Facilities were designed to achieve a target body temperature of 33 degrees Celsius, which would slow higher brain activity and allow the brain to repair any damage caused by oxygen deprivation.

CHESED was born 1.956 kg (4 pounds 5 ounces) and designated SCP-9220-A-607-B. In addition to the anticipated asphyxia, further complications arose immediately after the severing of the umbilical cord. An unaccountable amount of blood poured from the umbilical cord, originating from both CHESED and HASID. In addition to severe and dangerous levels of blood loss, the sudden outpouring of blood created physical problems for the researchers attempting to move CHESED to the cryogenic nursery. Once CHESED was moved, the team was able to staunch the bleeding by applying a torniquet to the umbilical cord.

CHESED had suffered extreme post-partum blood loss, and displayed symptoms of Grade 3 Hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy (HIE). Symptoms included: low heartbeat, no response to stimulation, chalky white skin tone, and difficulty moving limbs. CHESED entered seizure three times during the first 24 hours, and had to be under constant observation.

In spite of difficulties, CHESED was still alive after one week, and the remainder of the umbilical cord was successfully removed. The pregnancy was declared a success.

HASID's disposal was undertaken by Kraken. Immediately following this, Kraken requested reassignment and was moved to the SCP-████ project.


Addendum 9220.3: Collected Documentation on SCP-9220-A-607-B, "CHESED"


Disability Notice & Care Requirements for "CHESED"

This document is to remain up-to-date with CHESED's known disabilities, and current methods of care.

  • Spastic diplegia: Planned physical therapy includes: assisted and unassisted physical exercises, practice with both a wheelchair and forearm crutches, and equine-assisted therapy starting at the age of 5. Authorized personnel may contact Dr. L. Loudermilk with the Department of Massage Therapy for a detailed schedule.
  • Epilepsy: (Diagnosed 06/14/2032) CHESED displays three different kinds of seizures: absence (petit mal), atonic, and tonic-clonic (grand mal). CHESED regularly presents with absence seizures, with the most recorded at 43 in one day. Atonic and tonic-clonic are less common, but significantly more dangerous, and must be immediately reported at the first sign of onset.
  • Generalized depression: (Diagnosed 01/18/2036) CHESED is generally energetic, and enthusiastic about therapy assignments, but shows resistance to any long-term attachments. When playing with toys such as dolls or stuffed animals, CHESED does not attempt to name the toys or identify with them, and does not display preference for specific toys, as would be expected from other children of her age. She is likely to develop a major depressive disorder when she is older.
